rv.q: A swimming pool in Kansas, it turns out, is a sublime setting for the reclamation of joy.
The design elements support Greene’s work beautifully.

When she was growing up, Janice’s father Edwin (Biko Eisen-Martin) proudly regaled her with the tale of his adventure as a rambunctious youth sneaking into one of the white-only pools, which caused the city to shut it down for three days.“Why?” Janice asks“Sanitization. A Negro ‘infected’ the water they said.
The cast at Playwrights Horizons is tuned to each other like an orchestra, but in lesser hands, it's easy to see how the ripple could fall flat.

But, as with a lot of the intriguing notions floating around in the ripple… , such ideas are talked about more than dramatized, and Anderson’s labored poeticism prevents them from being as wrenching to us as they are to Janice.
A compelling family drama lurks inside the ripple, the wave that carried me home, but it cries out for fuller expression.
But in these pleasant, comparatively passive 90 minutes, it just stirs up a ripple.
A glorious kaleidoscope that you will not soon forget.
There's an undeniable power to her lyricism, and to the ways this production brings her ideas to the surface with theatrical originality.
The design is both practical and evocative, providing a visual continuity that complements the play’s movement through time.

cn.t: Critics find Christina Anderson's memory play affecting but uneven—its poetic exploration of civil rights-era pool segregation earns praise for intimacy and ambition, though some feel the script retreats from its own dramatic conflicts.

vr.q: a piece I'll be thinking about for quite some time
I may have gotten on the wrong train at the beginning of this play, but we all arrived at the same destination.
